subtitle: Midterm Important Subjective Questions (Solved)
topics: Financial Statements & Cost of Goods Sold

subjective.question: Define the following terms with examples: (1) Sunk cost (2) Implicit cost (3) Explicit cost (4) Opportunity cost (5) Historic cost. (Marks: 10)
subjective.answer: 1) Sunk cost: A cost that has been spent in the past and cannot be recovered; it should not be taken into account in management decisions. Example: stationery bought in bulk last month — the cost has already been incurred and is irrelevant to future decisions. 2) Implicit cost: The cost imposed on a firm for foregoing an alternative, where no actual payment is involved. Examples: use of the company's own capital, use of the owner's time, use of the owner's land in the business. 3) Explicit cost: A cost that involves actual payment, made now or payable in the future. Examples: payment for wages, rent or material; actual payment made to buy land for expansion instead of using the owner's land. 4) Opportunity cost: The benefit sacrificed by choosing one alternative over another — the cost of foregoing the next best alternative. Example: if the owner invests money in his business instead of keeping it in a savings account, the yearly bank interest forgone is the opportunity cost. 5) Historic cost: The cost incurred at the time of making a transaction, verifiable through a purchase agreement or invoice. It is used in financial accounting for valuing assets. Examples: cost paid to acquire land; cost incurred to buy machinery.

subjective.question: What is cost accounting? State its main purposes.
subjective.answer: Cost accounting is the process of accounting for costs — recording, classifying, allocating and analysing the costs of products, processes and departments so that the cost of each product or job can be ascertained and controlled. Its main purposes are: (1) to ascertain the cost of products, jobs and processes; (2) to provide information to management for decision making (pricing, make-or-buy, product mix); (3) to help in inventory valuation for financial statements; (4) to aid in the fixation of selling prices; (5) to control costs by comparing actual cost with standard/budgeted cost; and (6) to disclose profitable and unprofitable activities so that corrective action can be taken.

subjective.question: Differentiate between product cost and period cost, with examples.
subjective.answer: Product cost is the cost incurred to manufacture a product; it is attached to the units produced, becomes part of inventory value, and is charged to the income statement only when the units are sold (as cost of goods sold). Examples: direct material, direct labor and factory overhead. Period cost is the cost that is not related to production; it is charged to the income statement in full in the period in which it is incurred, because it expires with the passage of time. Examples: office rent, administrative salaries, selling and advertising expenses, interest expense.

subjective.question: PEL & Co. found that a production volume of 400 units corresponds to a production cost of Rs. 10,000 and a production volume of 800 units corresponds to a production cost of Rs. 12,000. Using the high-low method, calculate (i) the variable cost per unit and (ii) the total fixed cost.
subjective.answer: (i) Variable cost per unit = Change in total cost / Change in volume = (12,000 − 10,000) / (800 − 400) = 2,000 / 400 = Rs. 5.00 per unit. (ii) Total fixed cost = Total cost − Total variable cost (at 400 units) = 10,000 − (400 × 5) = 10,000 − 2,000 = Rs. 8,000. Check at 800 units: 8,000 + (800 × 5) = Rs. 12,000 ✓

subjective.topic: Financial Statements & Cost of Goods Sold
subjective.question: CK Products Limited purchased materials of Rs. 550,000 and incurred direct labor of Rs. 420,000 during the year ended June 30, 2006. Factory overheads for the year were Rs. 380,000. Inventory balances: Materials — July 1, 2005 Rs. 100,000, June 30, 2006 Rs. 105,000; Work in process — Rs. 121,000 and Rs. 110,000; Finished goods — Rs. 90,000 and Rs. 105,000. Required: (1) Cost of Goods Manufactured Statement (2) Cost of Goods Sold Statement. (Marks: 10)
subjective.answer: CK Products Limited — Cost of Goods Sold Statement for the year ended June 30, 2006: Opening inventory of materials: Rs. 100,000 Add: Purchases: Rs. 550,000 Less: Closing inventory of materials: Rs. 105,000 Direct material used: Rs. 545,000 Add: Direct labor: Rs. 420,000 Prime cost: Rs. 965,000 Add: Factory overhead cost: Rs. 380,000 Total factory cost: Rs. 1,345,000 Add: Opening work in process: Rs. 121,000 Less: Closing work in process: Rs. 110,000 Cost of goods manufactured: Rs. 1,356,000 Add: Opening finished goods: Rs. 90,000 Less: Closing finished goods: Rs. 105,000 Cost of goods sold: Rs. 1,341,000

subjective.topic: Financial Statements & Cost of Goods Sold
subjective.question: What is a Cost of Goods Manufactured (COGM) statement? Show its main components in order.
subjective.answer: The COGM statement is prepared by the cost accounting department to calculate the manufacturing cost of the goods completed during a period; it supports the cost of goods sold figure used in the income statement and final accounts. Its components, in order, are: (1) Direct material used (opening material inventory + net purchases − closing material inventory); (2) Add direct labor, giving prime cost; (3) Add factory overhead, giving total factory (manufacturing) cost; (4) Add opening work in process and deduct closing work in process, giving the cost of goods manufactured.

subjective.question: Define material control. Give the formulas for Re-order level, Minimum stock level, Maximum stock level and Danger level.
subjective.answer: Material control is the system that ensures materials of the right quantity and quality are available at the right time, without over-stocking or stock-outs, so that production continues smoothly at minimum inventory cost. Re-order level = Maximum consumption × Maximum lead (re-order) time. Minimum stock level = Re-order level − (Average consumption × Average lead time). Maximum stock level = Re-order level − (Minimum consumption × Minimum lead time) + Economic order quantity (re-order quantity). Danger level = Average consumption × Emergency lead time (time required for emergency purchase).

subjective.question: What is Economic Order Quantity (EOQ)? Give its formula and calculate the EOQ for a store that sells 5 cases of soda each day, where ordering cost is Rs. 8 per order, soda costs Rs. 3 per case, and daily holding cost is 5% of the cost of the soda.
subjective.answer: EOQ is the order quantity that minimises the total inventory cost (ordering cost + carrying cost) over the planning horizon; at the EOQ, total ordering cost equals total carrying cost. Formula: EOQ = √(2 × Annual usage × Ordering cost per order / Carrying cost per unit per year). Here: annual usage = 5 × 365 = 1,825 cases; carrying cost per case per year = 5% × Rs. 3 × 365 = Rs. 54.75. EOQ = √(2 × 1,825 × 8 / 54.75) = √(29,200 / 54.75) = √533 ≈ 23 cases.

subjective.question: Compare FIFO, LIFO and Weighted Average methods of inventory valuation. When prices are rising, which method gives the lowest gross profit, and why?
subjective.answer: Under FIFO (first in, first out), the earliest purchased units are issued first, so closing inventory is valued at the most recent prices. Under LIFO (last in, first out), the latest purchased units are issued first, so closing inventory is valued at the oldest prices. Under the weighted average method, issues are priced at a weighted average rate of all stock held. When prices are rising, LIFO gives the lowest gross profit: the most recent (highest) costs are charged to cost of goods sold, which increases COGS and reduces gross profit, while FIFO charges the older (lower) costs and reports the highest gross profit. (LIFO is not recommended under IAS 2.)

subjective.question: Differentiate between normal loss and abnormal loss and state the accounting treatment of each in cost accounting.
subjective.answer: Normal loss is the loss that is always expected and is unavoidable — it is inherent in the manufacturing process (e.g., evaporation of petrol during transportation). Abnormal loss is an unexpected loss that can be avoided by taking measures (e.g., loss by theft, fire or careless breakage). Treatment in cost accounting: normal loss is charged to the factory overhead (FOH) account and thus becomes part of the total production cost — it is absorbed by the good units, so the per-unit cost of good production increases. Abnormal loss is charged to the specific work in process / job account (and ultimately to the costing profit & loss account); it is not absorbed by good units, so the per-unit cost of good production is not affected by it.

subjective.question: What is the purpose of maintaining Job Time Sheets for workers in a manufacturing concern? (Marks: 5)
subjective.answer: The purposes of maintaining job time sheets for workers are: (1) preparation of payrolls, when the workers are paid on a time basis; (2) computation of overhead rates, if these are based on labor hours; (3) meeting statutory requirements; (4) differentiating between direct and indirect costs; (5) recording normal time, overtime, and regular and late comers; (6) administering increments, pension, provident fund, gratuity and other benefits; and (7) maintaining discipline and regularity and ensuring the daily requirement of the labor force in the factory.

subjective.question: Discuss the avoidable and unavoidable causes of labor turnover. (Marks: 10)
subjective.answer: Avoidable causes are those which can be removed by management action: (a) low wage rates in the organisation, so workers look for higher wages elsewhere; (b) dissatisfaction with the job; (c) bad working conditions; (d) long and odd working hours; (e) unsatisfactory relationship with supervisors; (f) bad relationship with fellow workers; (g) lack of adequate recreational facilities; (h) inadequate housing and medical facilities; (i) unfair methods of promotion and lack of promotion avenues; (j) lack of planning and foresight by management, seasonal nature of industry, non-availability of raw materials, power, etc. Unavoidable causes are those beyond management's control: (a) personal betterment of the worker; (b) retirement and death; (c) domestic responsibilities, e.g., looking after old parents; (d) workers leaving for personal reasons such as marriage, illness or relocation.

subjective.question: Define labor turnover and give the formulas of the three methods used to measure it.
subjective.answer: Labor turnover is the rate of change in the composition of the labor force of an organisation during a given period — i.e., the proportion of workers who leave and are replaced. 1) Separation method: Labor turnover = (Number of workers who left during the period / Average number of workers during the period) × 100. 2) Replacement method: Labor turnover = (Number of workers replaced during the period / Average number of workers during the period) × 100. 3) Flux method: Labor turnover = (Number of separations + Number of replacements) / Average number of workers × 100 (some versions take half of the combined figure). Average number of workers = (Workers at the beginning + Workers at the end) / 2.

subjective.question: A worker completes a job in 12 hours against a standard (allowed) time of 20 hours. The wage rate is Rs. 50 per hour. Calculate his total earnings under (i) the Halsey premium plan (50% bonus) and (ii) the Rowan premium plan.
subjective.answer: Time saved = 20 − 12 = 8 hours. Time wages = 12 × 50 = Rs. 600. (i) Halsey plan: Earnings = Time wages + 50% of time saved × rate = 600 + (0.50 × 8 × 50) = 600 + 200 = Rs. 800. (ii) Rowan plan: Earnings = Time wages + (Time saved / Time allowed) × Time wages = 600 + (8/20 × 600) = 600 + 240 = Rs. 840.

subjective.question: Define gross pay and net pay. Differentiate between statutory and non-statutory deductions with examples.
subjective.answer: Gross pay is the total earnings of an employee before any deduction; it includes basic pay, bonus pay and overtime payment. Net pay is the amount actually paid to the employee after all deductions: Net pay = Gross pay − Total deductions. Statutory deductions are those required by law, e.g., income tax deducted from the gross pay of an employee (the employer acts as an unpaid tax collection agent for the government) and employees' old-age benefits / social security contributions. Non-statutory deductions are voluntary or agreed deductions not required by law, e.g., provident fund subscriptions beyond the statutory requirement, union subscriptions, insurance premiums and loan repayments.

subjective.question: Irfan Industries Limited has two production departments A and B and two mutually interdependent service departments X and Y. Service department costs are apportioned as follows: X — to A 50%, B 30%, Y 20%; Y — to A 40%, B 50%, X 10%. Departmental costs after primary distribution: A Rs. 15,750; B Rs. 7,500; X Rs. 11,750; Y Rs. 5,000. Calculate the total factory overhead of the production departments using the repeated distribution method. (Marks: 5)

The budgeted factory overhead of a pharmaceutical company at two activity levels is: Low — 20,000 hours, Rs. 45,000; High — 40,000 hours, Rs. 75,000. Required: (i) Variable factory overhead absorption rate (ii) Budgeted variable factory overhead at the high activity level of 40,000 hours (iii) Budgeted fixed factory overhead. (Marks: 5)
subjective.answer: (i) Variable FOH rate = (Budgeted FOH at high level − Budgeted FOH at low level) / (High hours − Low hours) = (75,000 − 45,000) / (40,000 − 20,000) = 30,000 / 20,000 = Rs. 1.50 per hour. (ii) Budgeted variable FOH at 40,000 hours = 40,000 × 1.50 = Rs. 60,000. (iii) Budgeted fixed FOH = Total budgeted FOH at high level − Variable FOH = 75,000 − 60,000 = Rs. 15,000. (Check at low level: 45,000 − (20,000 × 1.50) = 45,000 − 30,000 = Rs. 15,000 ✓)

subjective.question: Ali Company estimates its factory overhead for the next period at Rs. 64,000. It is estimated that 30,000 units will be produced at a material cost of Rs. 65,000. Production will require 25,000 direct labor hours at an estimated cost of Rs. 130,000, and the machines will run about 18,000 hours. Required: the predetermined factory overhead rate based on (i) Units of production (ii) Direct labor hours (iii) Machine hours (iv) Direct labor cost (v) Material cost. (Marks: 5)
subjective.answer: Estimated factory overhead = Rs. 64,000. (i) Units of production basis: 64,000 / 30,000 units = Rs. 2.13 per unit. (ii) Direct labor hours basis: 64,000 / 25,000 hours = Rs. 2.56 per direct labor hour. (iii) Machine hours basis: 64,000 / 18,000 hours = Rs. 3.56 per machine hour. (iv) Direct labor cost basis: 64,000 / 130,000 × 100 = 49.23% of direct labor cost. (v) Material cost basis: 64,000 / 65,000 × 100 = 98.46% of material cost.

subjective.question: The Mars Company applies factory overheads to production by means of a predetermined rate based on expected actual capacity. Factory overhead at expected actual capacity of 120,000 hours is Rs. 240,000, of which Rs. 60,000 is fixed and Rs. 180,000 is variable. Normal capacity of the company is 150,000 hours. The actual capacity attained during the year was 100,000 hours and actual factory overhead was Rs. 180,000. Calculate: (1) the predetermined overhead rate based on expected actual capacity and on normal capacity; (2) the over-applied or under-applied factory overhead based on the rate used by the company. (Marks: 10)
subjective.answer: (1) Predetermined rate on expected actual capacity = Budgeted FOH / Expected actual capacity = 240,000 / 120,000 = Rs. 2.00 per hour. Predetermined rate on normal capacity = 240,000 / 150,000 = Rs. 1.60 per hour. (2) The company uses the expected-actual-capacity rate (Rs. 2.00). Applied FOH = Actual hours × Rate = 100,000 × 2.00 = Rs. 200,000. Actual FOH = Rs. 180,000. Since applied FOH (200,000) exceeds actual FOH (180,000), factory overhead is over-applied by 200,000 − 180,000 = Rs. 20,000.

subjective.question: Differentiate between allocation, apportionment and absorption of factory overheads.
subjective.answer: Allocation is the charging of discrete, identifiable items of overhead cost directly to the specific cost centres or cost units to which they wholly belong (e.g., the salary of a department's own supervisor charged wholly to that department). Apportionment is the division of overhead costs that cannot be identified with a specific cost centre among two or more cost centres, in proportion to the estimated benefit received, using a suitable basis or proxy (e.g., factory rent apportioned on floor area). Absorption is the final charging of the overheads of a production cost centre to the cost units (products) passing through it, by means of an overhead absorption rate (e.g., per direct labor hour or machine hour).

subjective.question: Differentiate between a blanket (single) overhead rate and departmental overhead rates.
subjective.answer: A blanket rate is a single overhead absorption rate established for the entire factory, based on the total factory overhead and total activity of the whole organisation; it is used to charge overheads to all products, whichever department they pass through. It is simple but can be inaccurate when products spend different lengths of time in different departments. Departmental rates are separate absorption rates computed for each production department, based on that department's own overhead cost and its own activity level and basis (e.g., machine hours in a machining department, labor hours in an assembly department). They measure each department's activity on an appropriate basis and ensure that the cost attributed to a cost unit reflects the departmental resources it actually used, so they give more accurate product costs.

subjective.question: What is meant by under-applied and over-applied factory overhead? How is the difference disposed of?
subjective.answer: Because factory overhead is applied to production using a predetermined rate based on estimates, the applied overhead usually differs from the actual overhead incurred. If the applied FOH is less than the actual FOH, the overhead is under-applied (under-absorbed); if the applied FOH exceeds the actual FOH, it is over-applied (over-absorbed). The difference arises from the spending variance and the capacity (volume) variance. Disposal: a small difference is written off to the income statement (cost of goods sold / net profit) of the period — under-applied FOH is subtracted from (charged against) profit and over-applied FOH is added to profit. A large difference, usually caused by abnormal factors, is prorated among work in process, finished goods and cost of goods sold.

subjective.question: Differentiate between process costing and job order costing. (Marks: 10)
subjective.answer: Process costing is a method of cost accounting applied to production carried out through a series of operations, stages or processes. Production is continuous, all units produced are similar (homogeneous), and the whole process is divided into several departments, with a separate process account for each process. Job order costing is the system that separately accumulates the costs incurred to produce each job, in a situation where each job is distinguishable from the others throughout the production process; the job may be a single unit, a multi-unit batch, a contract, a project or a service. It is employed where: (1) every order has its own manufacturing specifications, so every job is different and requires different amounts of material, labor and overhead; (2) each job is clearly distinguishable at all stages, making job-wise accumulation of cost possible; (3) each job is generally of high value; (4) production is generally in response to customers' orders; and (5) job-wise accumulation of cost is desirable or necessary for cost and profit determination. Job costing is more expensive as compared with process costing.

subjective.question: 50,000 units were received from the preceding department; 9,000 units were still in process at the end of the month (100% complete as to material, 75% complete as to labor and FOH). 500 lost units were 60% complete as to material and conversion costs; this loss is abnormal and is to be charged to factory overhead. Calculate the equivalent units of material, labor and factory overhead. (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: Units transferred out = Units received − Ending work in process − Abnormal loss = 50,000 − 9,000 − 500 = 40,500 units. Equivalent units of material = Transferred out + (Ending WIP × 100%) + (Abnormal loss × 60%) = 40,500 + 9,000 + 300 = 49,800 units. Equivalent units of labor and FOH = Transferred out + (Ending WIP × 75%) + (Abnormal loss × 60%) = 40,500 + 6,750 + 300 = 47,550 units.

subjective.question: Units transferred out to the next department were 20,000 units. Units lost at the beginning of production were 500 units. Units in process at the end were 2,500 units, complete as to materials and 1/2 complete as to labor and factory overhead. Prepare the Quantity Schedule. (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: Units to account for (started in process) = Transferred out + Units lost + Ending work in process = 20,000 + 500 + 2,500 = 23,000 units. Quantity Schedule: Units started in process: 23,000 Units accounted for as: — Transferred out to next department: 20,000 — Units lost at beginning of production: 500 — Ending work in process: 2,500 Total units accounted for: 23,000 ✓

subjective.question: Transferred out 22,000 units and units lost at beginning of production 500. Units in process at the end of the period were 2,500 units, complete as to materials and 1/2 complete as to labor and factory overhead. Compute the equivalent production of material, labor and FOH. (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: Units lost at the beginning of production have received no work, so they contribute no equivalent units. Equivalent production of material = Transferred out + (Ending WIP × 100%) = 22,000 + 2,500 = 24,500 units. Equivalent production of labor and FOH = Transferred out + (Ending WIP × 1/2) = 22,000 + 1,250 = 23,250 units.

subjective.question: Patacake Ltd produces a food item in a manufacturing process. On 1st November there was no opening stock in process. During November, 500 units of material were put into process at a cost of Rs. 9,000. Units completed and transferred out were 400 units. Direct labor cost in November was Rs. 3,840. Production overhead is absorbed at 200% of direct labor cost. Closing stock on 30th November consisted of 100 units, 100% complete as to materials and 80% complete as to labor and overhead. Required: the full production cost of completed units during November. (Marks: 5)
subjective.answer: Production overhead = 200% × 3,840 = Rs. 7,680. Total process cost = 9,000 + 3,840 + 7,680 = Rs. 20,520. Equivalent units: Material = 400 + (100 × 100%) = 500 units; Labor and overhead = 400 + (100 × 80%) = 480 units. Cost per equivalent unit: Material = 9,000 / 500 = Rs. 18; Labor = 3,840 / 480 = Rs. 8; Overhead = 7,680 / 480 = Rs. 16; Total = Rs. 42 per unit. Production cost of completed units = 400 × Rs. 42 = Rs. 16,800. (Value of closing WIP = (100 × 18) + (80 × 24) = 1,800 + 1,920 = Rs. 3,720; 16,800 + 3,720 = Rs. 20,520 ✓)

subjective.question: What is a job cost sheet? What information does it contain?
subjective.answer: A job cost sheet is the basic document of a job order costing system on which all costs incurred for a specific job are accumulated. A separate sheet is maintained for each job, identified by its job number. It contains: the job number, customer name and description of the job; the date started and the date completed; direct materials cost (from material requisitions); direct labor cost (from job time sheets); and factory overhead applied (activity base × predetermined overhead rate). The total of the three gives the total job cost, from which the cost per unit is computed by dividing by the number of units produced on the job. Selling and administrative costs are not shown on the job cost sheet, as they are period costs.

subjective.question: What is a cost of production report? What are its main parts?
subjective.answer: A cost of production report is prepared at the end of each costing period for each department (process); it summarises the quantity and cost data of the department for the period and serves as the source for journal entries transferring costs between departments and to finished goods. Its main parts are: (1) the quantity schedule — units to account for and units accounted for (transferred out, lost units, ending work in process); (2) the equivalent units of production for material, labor and overhead; (3) the cost per equivalent unit; and (4) the cost accounted for / cost reconciliation — the total cost assigned to units transferred out and to ending work in process, which must equal the total cost to account for.
